messages.body_plain:
Dear Julia,

You seen to have a shapefile issue (as well a minor units issue).

The easy part : I notice that the study region appears to be < 1 metre by 1 metre.

Looking at your map I see that the range is <1 in both the x (104.44 to 104.90) and y (-5.08 to -5.37) directions. I checked this by opening the map and reading the coordinates off the mouse location.

Next I checked your units.

File > Project Properties > Geographic

These were set to metres (you can change these here too as I am assuming they are incorrect.)

However, you do also seem to have a problem with your shapefile. I have tried a number of things to fix it. I imported it into R extracted the coordinates and re-made the shapefile using the shapefiles library. I did notice that there was a weird x and y limit on the coordinates. This could have been because the polygon was incomplete. I tried to fix this and the x and y limits made more sense. However, Distance is still not happy. I also tried importing your vertices by pasting directly into Distance so Distance created the shapefile. Again this did not fix the problem.

I therefore can only conclude that there is a problem with the vertices in your shapefile. Sometimes shapefiles become corrupted. Here are instructions to recover a corrupted shapefile  http://support.esri.com/technical-article/000007161

Alternatively you could just try creating the shapefile again.

Best wishes,

Laura

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Data results
messages.body_plain:
That is an unfortunate situation, Eric.

One possible cause is animal movement.  The area associated with the outer-most bins of point transects is large.  If animals are moving through your points, they might be detected in those outer bands; giving rise to the phenomenon in your data.  The longer the duration of your "snapshot" count, the more individuals accumulate in the outer bands.  Have a look at Buckland's (2006) Auk paper about point transect sampling methodology.

If you measured the time during your count when detections were made, you might be able to truncate detections made after some number of minutes; reducing the effect of animal movement through your point stations.  Other than that, I don't know of a "normalisation" method to employ.

messages.subject: Multiple surveys over time
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am helping to design a survey of a small area where the available effort and spacing considerations will allow the placement of about 12 to 15 transects. The survey will be repeated monthly over a 6 month period, with one of the objectives being to look at seasonal change in density.

The survey will be designed in DISTANCE using equal spaced parallel lines.

My expectation is that we will have to use a pooled detection function for all the surveys, given the expected number of sightings per survey. However this should not be problematic as the same platform and observers will be used throughout.

My question is this: is it better to use a new realization of the design (i.e. different transects) for every survey, or to use the same one each time? My expectation is that it is better to use a new realization each time, so that encounter rate is independent for each survey, but there may be factors I am not considering. It is logistically inconvenient to change the design for each survey, so I would like to make sure it is the correct approach.

Thanks in advance,

Daniel Pike.

messages.subject: SECR Question
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I was curious to see if anyone has had any experience with spatially explicit capture-recapture methods that utilize acoustic detections, primarily from callback responses to a broadcasted call.  We are dealing with a farily cryptic avian species that is generally impossible to detect visually (other than by random chance), is relatively sparse in its distribution, and does not reliably produce calls for any extended period of time.  However, this species does respond fairly well to broadcasted calls, and general locations can be derived from this.  I am looking into methods for trying to determine density of this species and thought that SECR methods may provide a way to accomplish this.

Any information or guidance anyone could offer would be most welcome.  I know this creates another complication in an already complicated method, but wanted to see if it might be possible.

Thanks,

John Edwards

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Multiple surveys over time
messages.body_plain:
Daniel

You are on the low side for replicate transects as you know.  Nonetheless, the question you ask is a common one.

There is a bit of information on the subject in Section 7.8.3 of Buckland et al. (2001).

By placing survey effort in new locations each month, you are accomplishing better spatial representation in your repeated surveys.  However, this comes at the expense of adding spatial variability to the temporal variability you are trying to measure.

If your objective is *solely* monthly changes in density, then using new realisations will make monthly differences more difficult to detect because of the added spatial variability induced by the changing transect locations.  However, given you stated seasonal changes were "one of the objectives", I suspect there are further objectives that need to be weighed in the decision.

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am using N-mixture models to estimate site abundance for a grassland bird using a large, two-year data set. While I do have distances for each count, I am interested in using zero-inflated models in unmarked.
The distances to birds in our data set ranges from 0-330 m; however, I'd like to truncate the data to only include the area where detection probability is reasonably high.

I first truncated our data at the 95th percentile of distances, which leaves counts ranging from 0-200 m. Next, I fit half-normal and hazard-rate curves (figure attached). As you can see, detection for the lowest bin (0-25 m) is quite a bit less than 1.0. I realize that if I were to proceed with distance sampling for my analyses, I would want to omit the lower distances in order to meet the assumption that detection is 1.0 at 0 m.

My question is: if I am only using this technique to quantitatively select a cutoff value for my subsequent analyses, is it necessary to discard all the distances on the far left where detection is clearly not 1.0? When I adjust bin sizes, or omit chunks of data, the plot just starts to get noisy and doesn't really provide me with any better information. I also get plots where some distance classes (bins) rise far higher than 1.0 on the y-axis, which I'm not quite sure how to interpret...

Hopefully this post doesn't seem vague. I'd appreciate any thoughts on how and whether to proceed with fitting a detection curve for my purposes. Ideally I would only include data within the range of distances where p is >0.5. Unfortunately, that would mean including only data from ~25-100 m, and discarding >1,000 of 3,000 counts. :/

Thoughts? Thanks in advance!
Best,
Mark

Hi Mark, list,

There are a number of statements in your e-mail that require some feedback, even though this is not an answer to your question. It is really not clear to me why you would want to use an N-mixture model since you have distance sampling data, given that if the distance sampling assumptions hold, it should lead to abundance/density estimates without much effort. But since N-mixture models are not my thing, I'll leave you to it to understand if there might be issues in using this data set under that context. Others might be willing to comment further.

But I can tell a few things that don't seem to be adding up with your data and your suggested approach. You never mention the words line or point, so I do not know if you are talking about lines or point transects. But the difference is key. This could be good (or bad, not really possible to tell from a plot only!) point transect data with detection functions overlaid on it incorrectly or this could be line transect data with a severe assumption violation (and detection functions still overlaid incorrectly). I am assuming this plot was generated by you, not by software like R package Distance, because the scaling of the histogram bars does not add up with the data. The area of bars above the fitted lines should be equal to the area of the bars below the fitted line. Even then, regarding bars above 0, these do not really mean much. There have been previous posts on this topic, but in short, you cannot read probabilities from the the histogram bars, only the line gives you the probability of detection.

Further, you are mentioning the possibility of left truncating your data, and I would say that is rarely ever a good idea unless there is a good understanding why small distances are missing in the first place. Say a blind spot under a plane might be a good reason, but even then to use with care. Avoidance movement by birds, the usual culprit for low numbers close by, could lead to extremely biased inferences if left truncation is blindly used. So, again, I would say left truncation is a bad idea (this is a gross oversimplification of course, but saves about 95% of the problems!), unless carefully justified. Forgive the self-promotion of my own work, but you might want to look into this paper for an example of the issues involved in left truncation:

Marques, T. A. 2016 A comment on Horcajada-Sánchez and Barja (2015): a cautionary tale about left truncation and density gradients in distance sampling
Annales Zoologici Fennici 53: 52-54

Any way, it seems to me you have to understand your data first before doing any further modelling. Using only data from a range of distances from which p>0.5 seems ad hoc (why not p>0.42, p>0.6, p>0.9, or p>0.6783) And it is unclear to me how it will help you, and strong assumptions would be needed for using only the data from the 25-100m range.

hope this helps,

Tiago

messages.subject: Interpretation of zero variance from dsm.var.gam()
messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of zero variance from dsm.var.gam()
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I'm conducting density surface modeling analyses for eight species of seabirds in the Labrador Sea based on line-transect surveys from vessels of opportunity. From these analyses I have produced two seasonal map pages for each species showing 1) the predicted densities in each cell, and 2) the coefficient of variation (CV) for the prediction in each cell - the CV map for Dovekie is attached.  The CV is based on the variance computed using dsm.var.gam() in the DSM R package.

On the map, the dots show the location of each 2 km long segment  with the size representing the number of birds detected (segments with no Dovekies are colored grey). The first thing you'll notice is that seasonal survey coverage varied considerably  - but that's the reality of ships of opportunity.

My question is about interpreting the large white areas in the top two maps (spring and summer) where the CV (and thus the variance) in each cell is zero. In these areas we had either very little survey coverage and/or no observations. Does the CV of zero indicate "perfect prediction" in these areas or does it indicate a failure of dsm.var.gam() to properly estimate the variance in these areas?

In case it's relevant, the GAM for this species included smooths for (x,y), sea surface temperature, sea surface height anomaly, eddy kinetic energy, depth, slope, and distance to the 1000 m depth contour (which runs parallel to the coast roughly down the middle of the study area) and each smooth was allowed to vary by season.

Note, that I'm using the CV maps to indicate to the reader of our report where the predictions have acceptable precision - I don't expect to get sensible predictions of density in the areas where we have poor survey coverage, I just want to understand how to interpret the CV of 0.

On a related note, what level of precision would you consider "acceptable" for the predictions? Areas where the CV is less than 1? Less than 2? Or some other value?

Thanks in advance!

Dave Fifield

*sigh* I should have read the entire tread before replying.

As far as David’s question is concerned my answer would be that a CV of zero mean that the model is quite certain of these predictions in this area since the ratio of uncertainty (sigma) to the mean is quite low.

The caveat I would put on interpreting those maps is that you would need to make sure that the values you used to interpolate the predictions are within the bounds of the values you used to fit the model. In other words, if the SST values in your explanatory data  range between -5 and 5 you will have to make sure that the SST values you are using to make the predictions are within those bounds. Otherwise you might end up with either very very large predicted densities (which is easy to spot) …or very very small predicted densities (which is more difficult to spot).

I don’t know of any good rules of the thumbs for CV but it the past I usually aimed for my predictions achieve a CV below 1.

Hope that helps. Chris

messages.body_plain:
Michelle

There are several places online where you can find code to resample with replacement from the transects in your survey.  That is what would be required to produce a new dataset that could repeatedly be handed to "ds()" to create replicate density estimates.  If you pursue that line, we could provide some hints.

However, check a couple of issues before doing so: do you have ~20 transects from which to resample?  Having a small number of transects will not produce useful estimates of precision.  Are you sampling transects or points? Before finding a new tool for estimating precision, ask what the existing tool is telling you:  is most of the uncertainty in your density estimates coming from imprecision in parameters of the detection function, or from encounter rate variability?  That will give you some insight about the utility of a bootstrap.  Finally, it might actually be the case that your estimates have low precision; it might not be possible for analytical magic to reduce the uncertainty.
